$comment: THE SHARED CWD-RESOLUTION CORPUS. Two guards answer one question — 'which
file will this command actually execute?' — and this file is what keeps
their answers the same.
WHY TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS STILL EXIST. parity-safety-net.sh answers it in
POSIX shell, where follow_cd mutates file-scope state that follow_locate
reads. worktree-binding-guard.mjs answers it in Node. There is no call that
reaches from Node into a shell function's file-scope state, so this is not a
factoring somebody skipped: it is one idea that cannot cross a language
boundary as a function call. CodySwannGT/lisa#3952 records that plainly,
including that this is NOT unification and does not meet that ticket's
stated bar.
WHAT IT BUYS INSTEAD. Drift fails a test on the commit that causes it,
rather than surfacing later as a wrong verdict found by whoever is unlucky.
THE RESIDUAL, STATED RATHER THAN IMPLIED. A behaviour with no row here is
free to diverge. ADD A ROW WHEN YOU ADD A BRANCH. The corpus is only as
good as its rows, and nothing outside this sentence forces a new one.
WHAT THE ROWS ASSERT. The resolved PATH, never the exit code. The two
guards fail in deliberately opposite directions when resolution is
impossible — parity-safety-net refuses, because a destructive command it
cannot see is what it exists to stop; worktree-binding-guard fails open,
which is the doctrine every undecidable case in that file follows. Binding
them on the verdict would force one of them to be wrong.
ROWS MUST BITE, ON BOTH SIDES. A resolver can be wrong in two directions
and they need different rows, so `control` is one of three:
bites — a PRE-FIX implementation, one that resolves relative tokens
against the hook process's own cwd, gets this row wrong. Guards
the silent direction: a confident verdict about a file nobody was
about to run.
wall  — an OVER-EAGER implementation, one that refuses whenever any `cd`
was unreadable, gets this row wrong. Guards the loud direction: a
fail-closed floor turning into a wall, and a wall gets switched
off, which costs the whole guard.
holds — pins behaviour that must not change. Passes under both wrong
implementations, so it proves the resolver RAN, not that it bites.
scripts/check-cwd-resolution-corpus.mjs refuses a set missing `bites` or
`wall`, refuses any contract point with no row, and refuses any contract
point carried only by `holds` rows — a point pinned by nothing that fails
under a wrong implementation is documented, not pinned.

contract.1: A literal `cd` establishes an effective working directory that REPLACES the hook process's cwd for relative tokens. Not an extra candidate and not a fallback ordering — the ordering was #3933's entire defect.
contract.2: Relative `cd` targets compose against the directory in force; the last `cd` wins; the result is absolutized and lexically normalised.
contract.3: A `cd` whose target is not literal text marks the effective directory UNKNOWN, and a later relative token is NOT resolved. Not literal is: empty, a leading `-`, or containing `$`, a backtick, or a glob metacharacter (`*`, `?`, `[`, `{`). A bare `cd` is `$HOME` and therefore known; `~` and `~/…` expand from `$HOME` first.
contract.4: UNKNOWN is sticky only until the next resolvable `cd`. A good `cd` clears it.
contract.5: The rule is SCOPED. It bites only a relative token a command declares it executes. Absolute paths are untouched, and a `cd` with no executed file after it is untouched. That scoping is what keeps a fail-closed floor from becoming a wall.
contract.6: A nested script's own `cd` is saved and restored around the recursive walk: the child inherits the directory but cannot change the parent's.

placeholders.{session}: The worktree the session is in — where a pre-fix implementation always resolved.
placeholders.{foreign}: A sibling worktree of the same repository, holding its own copy of the same relative path.
placeholders.{home}: The value of $HOME for the guard process.

rows.why: The defect in one line. A pre-fix implementation names {session}/run.sh, a real and readable file that nobody was about to run.
A leading ./ is still relative. Spelling it explicitly must not change which directory it is relative TO.
Relative targets compose against the directory in force, so `..` walks out of the first `cd`, not out of the hook's own cwd.
A later `cd` replaces an earlier one. An implementation that accumulated bases rather than replacing them would answer {foreign} here and be wrong in the quiet direction.
The wrong copy does not have to live in another repository. A subdirectory of the session's own tree is enough.
The fail-closed floor. A pre-fix implementation answers {session}/run.sh with full confidence about a file it has no reason to believe in.
A glob names a set, and a set is not a directory. Picking the first match would be a guess wearing a resolution's clothes.
`cd -` is the PREVIOUS directory, which this guard never saw. Correctly uncertain rather than treated as a directory named '-'.
A bare `cd` is `cd "$HOME"`. Leaving the previous directory in place would resolve later tokens from a directory the shell has left.
Unknown must not poison the rest of the command. A guard that refused everything after one unreadable `cd` would be a wall, and a wall gets switched off.
An absolute path does not need a cwd. Refusing it because some earlier `cd` was unreadable would be the fail-closed floor turning into a wall.
The unchanged case, and the one most commands take. The fix must be invisible here or it has broken far more than it repaired.
Scope control. An unreadable `cd` only matters when something relative is executed after it; on its own it is an ordinary command and must stay one.

rows.why_not_node: worktree-binding-guard.mjs reads the script a command executes but does not recurse into what THAT script executes, so it has no parent walk for a nested `cd` to leak into. Asserting this against it would test a walk it does not have.
rows.why: nested.sh changes directory internally. The child inherits the parent's directory and cannot change it, so `run.sh` still resolves from {session}. Without save/restore, a `cd` inside a followed file silently re-points the rest of the outer resolution.
